copy.title: When an AI Agent Can Touch Hardware: Designing the Checks Between the Model and the Machine
copy.one_line_summary: A practical look at the checks I put between an AI agent and real hardware work, and how they behave when the evidence is stale, conflicting, or incomplete.
copy.abstract:
When I started letting an AI agent work inside a hardware-engineering environment, model accuracy turned out to be only half the problem. The harder question was what to do with a plausible answer when the evidence behind it was incomplete, stale, or tied to the wrong board revision.

In Hardware-Splicer, the model can inspect sources, plan work, and call engineering tools, but it cannot decide by itself that a component has been identified, that a revision is current, or that a physical action is approved. Those checks live in deterministic project state and a separate human approval step.

This talk walks through the design and the failures that shaped it: partial evidence, conflicting component identity, parser failure, attractive but wrong analogies, and stale revisions. I will show what the system blocks, what it allows to continue, and why I now evaluate agents with metrics such as abstention, recovery, false blocking, and task completion instead of only asking whether the final answer was correct.

Hardware-Splicer is the concrete test case, but the pattern applies to other tool-using agents that can change real state rather than merely answer a question. The goal is not to make the model infallible. It is to keep a model mistake from automatically becoming permission to act.
takeaways: Keep the model's proposal separate from system state and permission to act. A good-looking answer is still only a proposal until the rest of the system can support it.
Tie evidence to the exact object and revision it describes. Old or conflicting evidence should not quietly survive a change in the underlying work.
Test how the agent fails, not only whether it finishes. Abstention, recovery, false blocking, and intervention are useful production metrics alongside task completion.
copy.speaker_bio: Christopher Ongko is a master's student at Yuan Ze University in Taiwan. He builds AI-assisted research and engineering systems, including Hardware-Splicer, a hardware-engineering environment that keeps model suggestions separate from deterministic checks and human approval. His broader work includes research-data infrastructure and tools for tracking sources, revisions, and reproducibility.
copy.short_bio: Christopher Ongko is a master's student at Yuan Ze University in Taiwan building AI-assisted research and engineering systems. His current work includes Hardware-Splicer and research-data tools focused on reproducibility and traceable evidence.
session_flow: The problem I ran into when the agent could do more than answer questions.
What stays outside the model: project state, checks, evidence, and approval.
Five failure cases and what the system does with them.
What I measure now besides answer accuracy.
Where the same pattern is useful outside hardware.
nonclaims: Do not claim AWS services are currently part of Hardware-Splicer unless that becomes true.
Do not claim a live external model has already passed the frozen corpus.
Do not claim fresh physical correctness is already closed.
Do not present the system as a universally safe agent.
